new_statements.rule_in_words: In most Cuyonon dialects (Cuyo Island proper) the inherited Proto-Bisayan accent contrast has been lost and stress has been regularised onto the final syllable of every full (content) word, whatever the syllable shape (so the pan-Bisayan closed-penult rule does not apply to Kuyonon, p.50). Phonemic vowel length exists but arises from vowel coalescence after consonant loss (ka:pún ~ kaapún 'yesterday' vs kapún 'castrate') and is independent of stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed for Kuyonon (Zorc reconstructs PBS secondary accent on prepenults, p.201, but says nothing about secondary stress in Kuyonon).
new_statements.exceptions: Some Kuyonon communities on Busuanga Island (Coron area) still keep contrastive penult/ultima stress on words in isolation (Kuy-Busuanga búrak 'flower' vs burák 'foam', lápad 'wide' vs ləpád 'to fly'), though 'many other forms reflect the general loss of contrast' (p.217). Zorc attributes the loss to contact with Palawan languages lacking contrastive word accent (p.218). deVries & Roe 1966:274 note that pronouns 'often have their own stress' and the prefix maga- usually lacks primary stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: 'every full word' (content words), in isolation; Zorc adds that in all Bisayan dialects stress is also 'a syntactic feature, a means of counting the full words in a clause' and can be overridden by intonation (pp.50-51). Zorc's 1971 field-note forms (informants from Cuyo and Coron) carry mostly final acute accents, consistent with the statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Zorc's 'Kuy' = Kuyonon of Cuyo Island proper (informants from Cuyo, with Coron/Busuanga speakers for comparison), i.e. Glottolog cuyo1237. The statement is explicitly dialect-split: final stress 'in most dialects', while the Busuanga Island (Coron) communities retain the inherited penult/ultima contrast. Ratagnon (rata1245), treated by Reid 2017 (after Zorc 1974) as a third Cuyunon dialect, is a separate Glottolog languoid and is not covered by the statement. deVries & Roe's 'Cuyono' is the same language.
